info.bio: Mötley Crüe es una banda estadounidense de hard rock formada en 1981 en Los Ángeles, California por el bajista Nikki Sixx y el baterista Tommy Lee a la que más tarde se le uniría el guitarrista Mick Mars y el vocalista Vince Neil, que con más de 12 millones de copias vendidas sólo en Estados Unidos y más de 33 en todo el mundo, es considerada como una de las bandas más importantes de la escena «glam» tanto en los años 1980 como en la actualidad y como una de las más influyentes en la escena mundial.

scenes.name: Lite metal: pop metal y glam
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: El subgénero que, desde 1983-84, intensifica el polo melódico del heavy y lo mezcla con el hard rock, quitándole el grave grueso. Philip Bashe lo llamó «metal pop» y señaló a Def Leppard y Van Halen; otros ejemplos son Poison, Bon Jovi, Ratt y Cinderella. Sus detractores, el público tradicional y el del thrash, lo llaman «poseurs», «false metal», «nerf metal», «poodle bands» o «glam», motes que describen bien sus rasgos: falta de autenticidad, pelo cardado, ropa colorida en lugar del negro obrero. Voz dulce sin gruñidos, armonías al modo de Aerosmith y Kiss, letras de amor y lujuria con nombres de chica y, sobre todo, la power ballad, que entra en radios que excluían el heavy y gana público nuevo, como las versiones blancas de Pat Boone en los cincuenta. MTV impulsó mucho su desarrollo. Se queda con la herencia dionisíaca y elimina el caos: «lo realmente pesado se quita».
scenes.family: Lite metal: glam y pop metal

scenes.name: US Festival 1983 y el renacimiento del heavy
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: A principios de los ochenta la prensa rock habla de «revival» o «renacimiento» del heavy (Creem, octubre de 1980: el género «había hecho un Jesucristo»): nacen bandas en todo el mundo, las veteranas tocan para públicos mucho mayores y los medios se abren al metal. La señal más pública es el US Festival de 1983, patrocinado por Steve Wozniak: el día dedicado al heavy, con Ozzy, Judas Priest, Mötley Crüe, Scorpions, Quiet Riot, Van Halen y Triumph, reunió mucho más público que los otros dos.
scenes.family: Cultura metal: público, medios y conciertos

scenes.name: MTV y Headbangers Ball
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: MTV nace en agosto de 1981 y en dos años casi monopoliza el videoclip. El heavy, visual desde que Judas Priest se vistió de cuero, es un candidato natural: entre los primeros grupos emitidos están Quiet Riot, Mötley Crüe, Twisted Sister, Dokken y Scorpions, y la cuota de mercado del metal salta del 8 % en 1983 al 20 % en 1984 («MTV fue responsable del resurgir del heavy», dice Dee Snider). A principios de 1985 la presión fundamentalista lo recorta, pero en 1988 nace el programa nocturno «Headbangers Ball». MTV selecciona del metal lo compatible con un público juvenil general: hace del lite metal un coautor del género (pelo cardado, chico malo mono, chicas en el público) y empuja al thrash, casi ausente, a definirse como antítesis comercial. Los vídeos, rodados por directores de publicidad, cuestan cada vez más (190.000 dólares uno de Poison en 1989) y dejan fuera a las bandas pequeñas, convierten los conciertos en simulacros del vídeo y, al llevar el metal al salón familiar, despiertan a sus enemigos: la lista de los «Filthy Fifteen» del PMRC y el departamento de normas de MTV.
scenes.family: Cultura metal: público, medios y conciertos

scenes.name: Las discográficas: majors e indies del metal
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: En los setenta el heavy solo está en las multinacionales (AC/DC en Atlantic, Sabbath y Purple en Warner, Priest en Columbia), que lo promocionan con giras y aprecian que los fans compren también el catálogo antiguo. La crisis discográfica de 1979-82 vuelve a las majors cautas; firman solo bandas ya hechas y trasladan el coste de formarlas a las familias de clase media y a mánagers emprendedores (el primer disco de Mötley Crüe, de 1982, salió en su propio sello, Leathür). Surgen los sellos independientes, primero en Gran Bretaña siguiendo el ejemplo del punk: Music for Nations (Martin Hooker, ex de EMI) con su filial Under One Flag; en Estados Unidos Metal Blade (1983, con Slayer, y luego Death Records), Combat, New Renaissance, y Roadrunner/Roadracer, que acapara el thrash brasileño de Sepultura y Ratos de Porão. Las majors los usan como equipos filiales y se quedan con el lite metal; en 1990 seis conglomerados controlan el 94 % de las grabaciones y solo uno de los 47 discos de metal del Top 100 de 1987-89 salió en un indie. El productor gana poder: el metal exige discos pulidos y los productores especializados median entre la banda, el sello y el gusto del público.
scenes.family: Cultura metal: público, medios y conciertos

scenes.name: La bestia ha vuelto: OzzFest y las reuniones
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: A finales de siglo el metal vuelve a la corriente principal. Con el alternativo moribundo y la electrónica sin despegar, el público fiel sigue ahí: tres mil personas esperan cinco horas en un centro comercial de Chicago en 1998 a que Black Sabbath les firme discos. El detonante es el OzzFest de 1997, organizado por la mánager de Ozzy, que vende más que Lollapalooza con Pantera, Machine Head, Fear Factory, Type O Negative, Neurosis, tres cuartas partes de Black Sabbath y Marilyn Manson, cuyas provocaciones atraen protestas cristianas y titulares. Metallica vuelve a tocar su thrash en directo y en Garage Inc.; Judas Priest ficha a Tim «Ripper» Owens, cantante de una banda tributo llamada British Steel; Mötley Crüe recupera a Vince Neil, Kiss se reúne en 1998, Dickinson regresa a Iron Maiden y Black Sabbath hace en 1999 una gira de reunión con disco de oro. Weinstein ve en ese regreso el gusto «prole» de la cultura de fin de siglo, un contrapeso a la feminización del pop y la ansiedad milenarista: la bestia se niega a morir.

scenes.name: La edad de oro del heavy metal
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: El heavy metal renace en los mismos años que la new wave, aprovechando los sellos independientes: Motörhead (puente entre metal, Stooges/MC5 y punk), Judas Priest, Iron Maiden, Diamond Head, Def Leppard y, en EE UU, Van Halen. Entre 1982 y 1985 el subgénero gótico se convierte en «black metal» (Venom, Mercyful Fate, Celtic Frost, Helloween, Bathory). El pop-metal y el shock-rock (Twisted Sister, Mötley Crüe, Joan Jett, Bon Jovi, Savatage); la pompa y el doom (Manowar, Voivod, Saint Vitus, Pentagram); el metal progresivo (Living Colour, Queensrÿche, King's X, Pantera, Joe Satriani) y el «street sound» de Los Ángeles (Guns N' Roses, Jane's Addiction, Faster Pussycat).

podcast.title: Vehicular Manslaughter of Razzle (1984)
podcast.body: In 1984, Vince Neil and Razzle, the drummer for Hanoi Rocks, left a party in Neil's powerful 1972 Ford Pantera to get more alcohol. While driving 65 mph in a 25 mph zone, Neil hit a wet patch, crossed into oncoming traffic, and crashed into two cars. Razzle died in the hospital, and Neil suffered cuts and cracked ribs. "While going 65 in a 25 miles per hour zone, the Pantera hit a wet patch of pavement, it crossed over into the opposite lane and crashed into two cars traveling the other way."

podcast.title: Nikki Sixx's 1987 Overdose
podcast.body: On December 23, 1987, Mötley Crüe bassist Nikki Sixx experienced a severe overdose. His heart stopped, and he was clinically dead for two minutes, requiring two shots of adrenaline to be revived. "Nikki Sixth of Motley Crew needed two shots of adrenaline to restart his heart on December 23rd, 1987. He was gone for two minutes."

podcast.title: Hair Metal Aesthetic and Lifestyle
podcast.body: Motley Crue fully embraced the hair metal aesthetic, characterized by "sky high teased hair, terror tight leather pants, lots of metal studs, carefully done makeup," drawing influence from bands like Kiss and the New York Dolls, with David Bowie cited as a "babysitter." Beyond their look, the band famously "lived the part of the drug and alcohol fueled rock stars," embodying the chaotic image associated with the genre. "motley crew mic mars Tommy Lee niki six been snail they had been in bands before and they brought their very own diverse experience and look to the band we're talking sky high t's terror tight leather pants lots of metal studs carefully done makeup like kiss and the new york dolls had offspring in david bowie was the babysitter they didn't just look the part they lived the part of the drug and alcohol fueled rock stars."

podcast.title: Legal Consequences and Remorse
podcast.body: Neil was charged with vehicular manslaughter and drunk driving. He served 20 days in jail, completed 200 hours of community service, and was ordered to pay $2.6 million to the crash's other victims. Even Neil himself later admitted he should have received a much longer jail sentence than 20 days. "Neil was charged with vehicular manslaughter and drunk driving."

podcast.title: Nikki Sixx's Pyrotechnic Stage Antics
podcast.body: Nikki Sixx was known for his extreme stage antics, which included spreading gel on his leather pants and setting them on fire during live shows. This dangerous stunt became a signature element of Motley Crue's flashy performances, which also incorporated pyrotechnics and elaborate lighting, influencing other bands like Ratt, Poison, Warrant, and Dokken to emulate their look. "and yes niki six did spread a gel on his leather pants and set them on fire during live shows other bands would emulate the look rat poison warrant docken I could go on motley crews live shows were flashy to full of pyrotechnics and flashing lights and Tommy Lee being seat belted into his drum kit while he was lifted vertically toward the roof of the arena certainly their overall aesthetic reflected as writer calipa sonay put it the chaos of their own lives but as he also pointed out in major labels the music of motley crew and other hair metal bands was not really that scary they sang these great arena anthems and if they wanted to continue to draw in the female audience it certainly helped to have a power ballad you know that's when the lead singer would show his sensitive side or motley crew it was home sweet home on nineteen eighty five's theater of pain but even these power ballots are going to smooth out let's listen first to a bit of home sweet home and I'm coming on this home sweet home that song is made to be sung in auditorium's and arenas I can see all the lighters now there's nothing about it that is the exclusive domain of misunderstood sixteen year old white kids it had mass appeal this is from the August nineteen eighty seven Alan town Pennsylvania newspaper we have great admiration for our fans niki six says and we don't care about MTV or radio or whether critics like us or don't like us it just doesn't matter to us what matters is when the kids make home sweet home the number one song on the request line for five months on MTV that's something that no one but the kids do and that floors me."

xref.body: A trip to India sparked a spiritual awakening for Anthony Kiedis. Upon returning to Los Angeles in 1997, he checked into a "last chance" rehab place called the Impact Drug and Alcohol Treatment Center in Pasadena for about a month, a facility known for hosting members of Mötley Crüe and Brent Gerowicz of Bad Religion. xref.title: Battle of Bands Win Led to Bob Rock's First Ever Production Credit
xref.body: The band started as the K-Tels in 1978 in Vancouver but were threatened with legal action by the cheap record company K-tel International and renamed themselves Young Canadians. Frontman Art Bergman would remain a presence in Canadian alt-rock for decades, ultimately being made a Member of the Order of Canada in 2020. The band won a local Battle of the Bands contest that awarded them studio time at a new facility called Little Mountain Sound. The engineer assigned to these unknown contest winners was a young man named Bob Rock — it was the first time Rock ever produced anything. He went on to produce Metallica, Mötley Crüe, Bon Jovi, The Cult, the Tragically Hip, and many others. "The engineer assigned to them was some kid named Bob Rock."

xref.body: Samantha Maloney was a member of Hole, with Courtney Love, and notably filled in for Tommy Lee in Mötley Crüe when he was temporarily unable to perform. This demonstrates her versatility and high demand as a drummer. "Samantha even filled in for Tommy Lee and Motley Crew when he was out of action for a while."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Career Ignored in Los Angeles
xref.body: In their early days, the band was largely ignored in Los Angeles because their sound did not align with the popular bands of the time, such as Guns N' Roses and Mötley Crüe. "Their sound really didn't fit in with everything else that was happening in Los Angeles. Everyone wanted bands. It sounded like guns and roses and motley crew."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Sound and Image Shift
xref.body: The original Alice in Chains had a sound more akin to Van Halen and Mötley Crüe than Grunge. However, they underwent a change of image and sound tweaks when the Seattle grunge scene began to emerge, which proved to be a successful move for the band. "The original Allison Chains was more Van Halen and Motley Crude than Grunge. But then, when everybody realized what was going on around them in Seattle, there was a change of image and a couple of sound tweaks."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Tattoo Glorification in Hair Metal
xref.body: LA Guns is noted among bands of the hair metal era, such as Mötley Crüe and Guns N' Roses, that explicitly glorified tattoos. This was integral to the visual impact and aesthetic of the time, complementing other elements like elaborate hair, makeup, and fashion. "So in the 80s, bands like Molly crew, Guns and roses, LA guns, they glorify tattoos. Right up front."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock'n'Roll Tattoos

xref.title: Unique Rock and Roll Philosophy
xref.body: In the early 1990s, the Manics distinguished themselves by professing to have more in common with American hard rock bands like Guns N' Roses and Motley Crue than with bands from Manchester or the emerging Britpop scene. They openly bragged about wanting to sell millions of records, a desire uncommon among indie bands of that era, and readily signed with a major label. "The Manics were different for the early 1990s. They professed to have more in common with guns and roses in Motley Crew than anything from Manchester or early Britpop, saying that real rock and roll came from America."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
